units.translation: 802. Or also a chest: now he means the basket, and this is clear from “having placed it on her knees.” Eratosthenes etymologizes “chest” in the Hermes (fr. IV Hiller): “They named it a chest, because it hid the stolen prey; from this it is called a chest among men.”

807. Incorrectly the correlative τόφρα is used instead of ὄφρα, “in order that”: “so that the race may not be without seed” (Υ 303). 〈Properly〉 it is equivalent to τέως, as “while, until.” Homer clarifies it well (Θ 66 sq.): “While it was morning and the day was waxing—, so long the missiles of both sides flew thick.” The form πάσαιτο is sound; for its substitution does not lead to satiety.

846-47 a. Δαῖραν μουνογέ〈νειαν〉: Δαῖραν is an ellipsis of the ε for the sake of the meter; for it is Δάειραν. He means Persephone, as the word μουνογένειαν shows. He called her Νυχίαν either because she rules over the underworld—for they call the lightless place “night”—or because she is propitiated when it is night; for it is reasonable that the ruler of the nether regions is propitiated at the hour of night. That they call Persephone Δαῖρα, Timosthenes in his Exegeticus (fr. 12 Tresp, Die Fragm. d. gr. Kultschr. 1914, 52) agrees, and Aeschylus in the Psychagogi (fr. 277 N.²) indicates it, understanding Persephone as Δαῖρα.
